We select category zero first. PyTorch chooses its implementation; the diagram follows our flag, scan and scatter construction.
spokenForms.compaction__s02-c1: Exclusively scan the keep flags. Each offset counts selected tokens strictly before that input position. A kept token uses its offset as an output destination. A skipped token performs no output write, even if its offset matches another token's offset.
spokenForms.compaction__s02-c2: The flags and all offsets must finish before placement starts. For this non-empty input, add the last exclusive offset and last flag to obtain the output count. The teaching model reserves eight slots and reports the used prefix; it does not model PyTorch's allocation strategy.
spokenForms.compaction__s03-c1: Scatter writes an input item to a calculated destination. Token five is highlighted in the input row. It has two earlier survivors, so its completed exclusive offset gives it output slot two. Its thread copies the token identity into that slot.
spokenForms.compaction__s03-c2: The output picture shows only writes inspected so far; a question mark labels an unwritten slot. Every kept thread has a distinct destination. This destination contract, rather than the bounds guard alone, prevents conflicting writes and preserves survivor order.
spokenForms.compaction__s04-c1: Inspect the same valid placements in reverse input order. The destinations do not change because they came from the completed scan. A later input may write first without taking an earlier token's output slot.
spokenForms.compaction__s04-c2: The completed token identities match forward inspection and retain input order. These are two chosen valid write sequences, not a GPU scheduling prediction. A block barrier cannot finish a scan produced by other blocks; dependent phases need the required wider ordering.
spokenForms.compaction__s05-c1: Now keep tokens whose category differs from zero. Leave the input identities and reverse inspection order unchanged. Predict the output identities, and derive the destination used by token four.
spokenForms.compaction__s05-c2: Would writing the last surviving token first change its final output position? Explain why matching the old survivor count would not prove that the correct identities were selected. Pause before the comparison.
spokenForms.compaction__s06-c1: Four tokens survive this new selection. Their identities remain in original relative order, as shown in the output. Token four has two earlier survivors, so its destination is two. Reversing the inspected writes changes neither that destination nor stability.
spokenForms.compaction__s06-c2: A skipped thread never writes. With an empty selection, all threads skip and no output slots are used; that differs from an empty input. Return to the chapter to inspect destinations and test all or no survivors. No GPU runtime, allocation cost or speedup is inferred from these placements.
spokenForms.devices__s01-c1: Chapter Two starts with five floating-point values stored in system [RAM](/ˌɑɹ ˌeɪ ˈɛm/), separate from the CPU processor. The CPU runs Python and requests GPU operations.
spokenForms.devices__s01-c2: In this discrete GPU, the compute chip and dedicated GPU memory are separate. The chip reads inputs, multiplies them and writes results. A transfer copies values between system [RAM](/ˌɑɹ ˌeɪ ˈɛm/) and GPU memory.
spokenForms.devices__s02-c1: Calling the tensor's to method with [CUDA](/ˈkuːdə/) as the destination requests a GPU copy. PyTorch arranges storage and copies five values: twenty bytes of tensor data.
spokenForms.devices__s02-c2: The original CPU tensor still exists. The copy contains the same numbers in different storage; copying has not doubled them.
spokenForms.devices__s03-c1: Multiply the GPU tensor by two. The result, y GPU, has its own GPU storage. The input x GPU keeps its original values.
spokenForms.devices__s03-c2: This operation copies zero bytes between CPU and GPU. That does not mean zero memory activity: the calculation still reads inputs and writes outputs in GPU memory.
spokenForms.devices__s04-c1: Calling CPU on the result requests a CPU copy. The values two, four, six, eight and ten now also have storage in system [RAM](/ˌɑɹ ˌeɪ ˈɛm/).
spokenForms.devices__s04-c2: Twenty bytes cross back in this example. The GPU result remains on the GPU; PyTorch does not automatically move every calculation's result to the CPU.
spokenForms.devices__s05-c1: Across this sequence, twenty bytes of tensor data go in, zero cross during multiplication, and twenty come back. That is forty bytes copied between devices.
spokenForms.devices__s05-c2: These are payload counts for the chosen example. They exclude other traffic and overhead, and they do not tell us how long the operations take.
spokenForms.devices__s06-c1: If another calculation needs the GPU result, it can read it there. A CPU copy is needed when a CPU-side consumer needs the values.
spokenForms.devices__s06-c2: Choosing where to keep values can avoid unnecessary round trips. Whether that improves an application's speed depends on its actual operations and measurements.
spokenForms.devices__s07-c1: Try eight values instead, each still using four bytes. The GPU has multiplied them by three. Now request a CPU copy of y GPU.
spokenForms.devices__s07-c2: Which values appear in the CPU result, and how many bytes of tensor data cross back? Does this copy change the original CPU input? Pause and explain the storage locations.
spokenForms.devices__s08-c1: The CPU result contains three, six, nine, twelve, fifteen, eighteen, twenty-one and twenty-four. Eight values at four bytes each means thirty-two bytes copied back.
spokenForms.devices__s08-c2: The original CPU input is unchanged. Return to Chapter Two and trace which operation creates each destination tensor, separating copies from calculation and from timing claims.
spokenForms.divergence__s01-c1: Chapter Eight follows a conditional calculation: double positive inputs and negate negative inputs. A lane mask is the set of lanes participating in one issued operation.
spokenForms.divergence__s01-c2: Begin with thirty-two inputs, all positive two. Every lane takes the positive path, producing four. The negative path is empty, so this arithmetic model skips it. The trace lists arithmetic only, not loads, stores or branch overhead.
spokenForms.divergence__s02-c1: Now alternate positive two and negative two across the full warp. Divergence means participating lanes of one warp take different paths through a condition.
spokenForms.divergence__s02-c2: The model starts with the positive path: lanes zero, two, four, and the other even positions multiply by two. The white lanes have inputs for the other path; they do no arithmetic in this operation.
spokenForms.divergence__s03-c1: Next, the negative mask selects lanes one, three, five, and the other odd positions. Negating their negative-two inputs produces positive two. The positive lanes do no arithmetic during this operation.
spokenForms.divergence__s03-c2: Both paths have participating lanes, so both appear. Positive-first ordering is a teaching choice. PyTorch chooses its implementation; the conditional expression alone does not establish a compiled branch or this operation order.
spokenForms.divergence__s04-c1: Change to one negative input, in lane zero. The positive path serves the other thirty-one lanes. A path needed by one lane still has a non-empty mask.
spokenForms.divergence__s04-c2: Lengthen the negative expression to negate, multiply by two, then add one. Those three operations each use lane zero's mask, producing five. Alongside the positive multiply, the trace contains four arithmetic operations, not a measured GPU duration.
spokenForms.divergence__s05-c1: Return to five all-positive inputs. Lanes zero through four participate in the positive multiply. The remaining twenty-seven positions have no input throughout this calculation.
spokenForms.divergence__s05-c2: This low participation does not mean divergence: every participating lane takes the same path. An unused position is different from a lane waiting for its own path. Other blocks' threads do not fill the empty positions in this warp.
spokenForms.divergence__s06-c1: Keep five inputs and change only their signs to alternating. Lanes zero, two and four use the positive path; lanes one and three use the negative path.
spokenForms.divergence__s06-c2: Positions five through thirty-one remain unused for both operations. White cells identify participating inputs on another path; dashed cells identify positions with no input. Inspect the masks to explain low participation instead of guessing its cause.
spokenForms.divergence__s07-c1: Apply the mask rule to a new case. Lanes zero through fifteen have positive two, lane sixteen has negative two, and the remaining positions have no input.
spokenForms.divergence__s07-c2: The positive expression doubles its input; the negative expression negates, doubles, then adds one. Predict which operations appear and the lane mask for each. Pause before revealing the trace.
spokenForms.divergence__s08-c1: The positive multiply uses lanes zero through fifteen. All three negative operations use lane sixteen. There are four issued arithmetic operations, and positions seventeen through thirty-one are unused throughout.
spokenForms.divergence__s08-c2: The positive results are four and the negative result is five. Return to Chapter Eight and separate other-path lanes from unused positions. These explicit arithmetic masks do not establish compiler lowering, hardware path order or elapsed GPU time.
spokenForms.hello__s01-c1: Chapter One starts with five floating-point inputs: one, two, three, four and five. Doubling gives two, four, six, eight and ten.
spokenForms.hello__s01-c2: PyTorch chooses the implementation for its tensor operation. Our manual [CUDA](/ˈkuːdə/) example performs the same calculation, so we can trace how each result is produced.
spokenForms.hello__s02-c1: A thread is one execution of a GPU program. In this example, each participating thread reads one input, doubles it and writes the matching output position.
spokenForms.hello__s02-c2: Thread four reads input index four, whose value is five. It writes ten at output index four. An index chooses a position; it is not the stored value.
spokenForms.hello__s03-c1: With four threads per block, local positions start again at zero in each block. Block one, position zero therefore needs a global array index.
spokenForms.hello__s03-c2: Multiply the block number by the block size, then add the local position. One times four plus zero gives index four, so this thread doubles the fifth input.
spokenForms.hello__s04-c1: The CPU requests two blocks of four threads and passes an input count of five. The eight launched threads have indices zero through seven.
spokenForms.hello__s04-c2: The count is an ordinary kernel argument supplied by the CPU program. Changing the number of blocks does not change that count or allocate longer arrays.
spokenForms.hello__s05-c1: The correct check permits only indices smaller than five: zero through four. Threads five, six and seven skip both the read and the write.
spokenForms.hello__s05-c2: A check allowing index five would access positions that do not exist. The guard trusts the supplied count; the CPU must also provide enough input and output storage.
spokenForms.hello__s06-c1: Now there are nine inputs, with indices zero through eight. Keep four threads per block. Would two blocks cover every input?
spokenForms.hello__s06-c2: Predict the smallest block count that covers all nine values. Which launched indices must then skip the arrays? Pause before comparing.
spokenForms.hello__s07-c1: Two blocks create only eight threads, leaving input index eight without a thread. Three blocks create twelve threads, covering all nine inputs.
spokenForms.hello__s07-c2: With the count set to nine, indices nine, ten and eleven skip the arrays. A bounds check can prevent an access, but it cannot create a missing thread.
spokenForms.hello__s08-c1: Keep three questions separate: which input does this thread select, how many threads did the CPU launch, and which indices may safely access the arrays?
spokenForms.hello__s08-c2: Return to Chapter One and compare four with eight threads per block. Explain why the grouping changes while each valid input still produces the same doubled result.
spokenForms.histograms__s01-c1: Chapter Fifteen counts destinations chosen for eight tokens. A token's category identifies its counter; its input position identifies the token. Several threads may choose the same counter.
spokenForms.histograms__s01-c2: The diagram keeps those identities separate. Each category's counter is called a bin. Every input contributes exactly once. The four counters begin at zero, and their final counts must add up to eight.
spokenForms.histograms__s02-c1: An atomic addition combines reading a counter, adding one and writing it back as one indivisible update. This protects the count when multiple threads target the same location.
spokenForms.histograms__s02-c2: The highlighted thread contributes to its selected category. These arrows show logical destinations, not simultaneous hardware execution. Atomic addition does not provide a block barrier or order every unrelated memory access.
spokenForms.histograms__s03-c1: Give each block its own shared counters for its four threads. Each block initialises them, reaches a barrier, performs local atomic updates, then reaches another barrier before merging.
spokenForms.histograms__s03-c2: For the mixed input, the first block has three non-zero bins and the second has three. Merging only non-zero partial bins needs six global atomic additions, plus eight local atomic additions.
spokenForms.histograms__s04-c1: Now route every token to category zero. There are still eight tokens. With global counters, each token needs an atomic addition, and every addition targets the same counter.
spokenForms.histograms__s04-c2: This concentration changes contention: several threads request the same location. The model reports counts and operation totals. It assigns no atomic latency and cannot establish a measured slowdown.
spokenForms.histograms__s05-c1: Keep the same eight category-zero tokens and two blocks of four. Change only counter ownership to separate block partials, then merge only non-zero bins.
spokenForms.histograms__s05-c2: Predict the number of global atomic additions. Also name the extra work that prevents this count alone from proving a faster kernel. Pause before the comparison.
spokenForms.histograms__s06-c1: Each block counts four tokens into its own counter for category zero. Only one partial bin in each block is non-zero, so merging needs two global atomic additions. Category zero receives all eight contributions; every other counter stays zero.
spokenForms.histograms__s06-c2: Local atomics, shared storage, initialisation, barriers and merging still cost work. Return to the chapter to compare distributions and explain your hypothesis. Operation counts are not measured GPU times or guaranteed speedups.
spokenForms.inference__s01-c1: Chapter Thirteen connects cached keys and values to inference budgets. A decoder reuses these stored tensors when processing a later token. This model-managed cache is separate from the GPU's hardware caches.
spokenForms.inference__s01-c2: The chapter opens with a small PyTorch append example. Our budget instead uses a synthetic decoder: thirty-two layers, seven billion parameters, and two-byte weights and cache values. These are declared assumptions, not a named model or measured GPU.
spokenForms.inference__s02-c1: Start with one sequence and five hundred and twelve cached tokens. Each layer stores a key and a value, each with one thousand and twenty-four components, for every token. Multiply all those counts by two bytes per value.
spokenForms.inference__s02-c2: The existing payload is sixty-four mebibytes. One mebibyte means one million, forty-eight thousand, five hundred and seventy-six bytes. This is occupied payload, excluding spare allocation and metadata. Capacity alone does not tell us how much work an invocation performs.
spokenForms.inference__s03-c1: Decode processes one new token for each sequence. Here the cache grows from five hundred and twelve to five hundred and thirteen tokens. The budget reads the existing sixty-four mebibytes and writes one hundred and twenty-eight kibibytes of new keys and values.
spokenForms.inference__s03-c2: It also counts one read of the fourteen-gigabyte weight payload. Gigabytes here are decimal; cache mebibytes and kibibytes use powers of two. The budget excludes activation transfers and other work. These are selected model counts, not a capture of actual memory traffic.
spokenForms.inference__s04-c1: Prefill processes all five hundred and twelve prompt tokens from an empty cache. It reads no previous cache entries and writes the whole sixty-four-mebibyte payload. The ideal weight read is still fourteen gigabytes, shared across the invocation.
spokenForms.inference__s04-c2: Arithmetic increases because many tokens are processed. Dense-weight work grows with token count; attention work also grows with context. This synthetic count uses a hidden width of four thousand and ninety-six and full square prompt attention, without causal triangular savings.
spokenForms.inference__s05-c1: Assume one thousand decimal gigabytes per second and one hundred trillion floating-point operations per second. A floating-point operation is one arithmetic operation in this count. Divide the selected bytes by bandwidth and the operation count by compute rate.
spokenForms.inference__s05-c2: For decode, the memory bound is about fourteen point zero six seven milliseconds and the compute bound about zero point one four three. Prefill's compute bound rises to about seventy-three point zero five four. Take the larger bound, not their sum. These are ideal minimum budgets, not elapsed-time predictions.
spokenForms.inference__s06-c1: Increase decode batch from one sequence to four, keeping five hundred and twelve cached tokens per sequence. The ideal model shares the same weight read across the batch. Each sequence still needs its own cache, and total arithmetic grows.
spokenForms.inference__s06-c2: The invocation bound grows slightly, while dividing it by four gives about three point five six seven milliseconds per produced token. That is an amortised budget, not one user's next-token latency or measured throughput. These are four independent sequences, not four successive tokens from one sequence.
spokenForms.inference__s07-c1: Keep the four independent decode sequences. Change only their previous cache length from five hundred and twelve to two thousand and forty-eight tokens each. Keep the same layers, widths, value size, parameters and rates.
spokenForms.inference__s07-c2: Predict the existing cache payload. Must the whole invocation's ideal lower bound also grow fourfold? Separate the old cache read, each sequence's new entry and the shared weight read. Pause before comparing the answer.
spokenForms.inference__s08-c1: The cache grows from two hundred and fifty-six to one thousand and twenty-four mebibytes. The new entries stay five hundred and twelve kibibytes in total, and weights stay fourteen gigabytes. Recomputing both bounds gives about fifteen point zero seven four milliseconds, not four times the earlier bound.
spokenForms.inference__s08-c2: Under these assumptions the weight read still dominates counted bytes. This does not identify a real GPU bottleneck. Return to Chapter Thirteen and distinguish capacity, work per invocation and ideal time limits. A real timing comparison needs a named model, implementation, timing scope and repeated hardware measurements.

spokenForms.inside-sm__s01-c5: The input and output arrays are in GPU memory, outside the S M.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s02-c1: Thread Zero’s load requests the value at input index zero.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s02-c2: Load and store units handle memory instructions.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s02-c3: A load brings a value from memory into a register: a small, fast storage location inside the S M.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s02-c4: Registers hold the working values that arithmetic instructions use.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s02-c5: The request can take time; this diagram jumps ahead to when one point zero arrives in a register.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s02-c6: The input array still holds its original value.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s02-c7: Nothing has been written to the output array yet.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s03-c1: The multiply instruction uses the loaded value and the multiplier two.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s03-c2: Floating point arithmetic units perform calculations on floating point values.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s03-c3: Here, they produce two point zero and return the result to a register.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s03-c4: Our values use thirty two bit floating point, often called F P thirty two.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s03-c5: These arithmetic units are shared by threads, rather than permanently owned by Thread Zero.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s03-c6: The multiply has not written the result to the output array.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s04-c1: The store is a separate instruction.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s04-c2: Load and store units write two point zero from the thread’s result register into output index zero in GPU memory.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s04-c3: The result is now in the output array.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s04-c4: We have followed the whole value path: memory to register, arithmetic, then register to memory.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s05-c1: Now inspect Thread One, whose input is two point zero.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s05-c2: Its load supplies its own working register.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s05-c4: We are changing which values we inspect, not choosing the GPU’s execution order.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s05-c5: A GPU can execute instructions for groups of threads together; this picture isolates two threads to make their values easy to follow.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s06-c1: Thread One’s multiply uses the same depicted floating point hardware, producing four point zero.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s06-c2: Its store writes that result to output index one.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s06-c3: Each thread has its own working values, while execution units are shared.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s06-c4: The input and result columns identify values, not fixed physical registers.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s06-c5: A register can be reused after a value is no longer needed.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s06-c6: The boxes show hardware roles, not unit counts or exactly when instructions execute.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s07-c2: A third thread loads three point zero and multiplies it by two.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s07-c3: Its store instruction has not run.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s07-c4: Where is the result at this point: in a working register, or in the output array?
spokenForms.inside-sm__s08-c1: The result, six point zero, is in a working register.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s08-c2: The store is what writes it to the output array.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s08-c3: That is the distinction to take back to Chapter One: threads describe executions with separate working values.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s08-c4: The S M provides shared hardware for loads, arithmetic and stores.
spokenForms.inside-sm__s08-c5: This is a conceptual explanation, not a trace of the kernel PyTorch selected.
spokenForms.launch-from-input__s01-c1: Chapter Three follows the manual [CUDA](/ˈkuːdə/) workflow for the same five inputs. The CPU program already has a vector containing those values.
spokenForms.launch-from-input__s01-c2: It obtains the element count from the vector size and passes that count to the kernel. A GPU pointer carries an address, not an automatically discoverable array length.
spokenForms.launch-from-input__s02-c1: The element count is five. Each F P thirty two value occupies four bytes, so each five-element array needs twenty bytes of value storage.
spokenForms.launch-from-input__s02-c2: Allocation and copy calls take byte counts. The kernel bounds check takes an element count. For this one-input, one-output operation, both arrays have the same number of positions.
spokenForms.launch-from-input__s03-c1: The CPU allocates twenty bytes for GPU inputs and twenty bytes for GPU outputs. Allocation reserves storage; it does not copy the CPU vector values.
spokenForms.launch-from-input__s03-c2: A host-to-device copy then fills the GPU input allocation. The kernel will write the separate output allocation. The original CPU input remains available.
spokenForms.launch-from-input__s04-c1: Choose four threads per block for tracing. Round the input count up to whole blocks: five inputs need two blocks, creating eight threads.
spokenForms.launch-from-input__s04-c2: The CPU passes the GPU pointers and element count as ordinary arguments. The bounds check permits indices zero through four and excludes the three extra threads.
spokenForms.launch-from-input__s05-c1: After the kernel, a device-to-host copy places five results in a CPU output vector. This blocking copy in the default stream completes the preceding calculation before the CPU uses those results.
spokenForms.launch-from-input__s05-c2: The program checks the result and frees both GPU allocations. Freeing GPU storage does not erase the CPU result or the original CPU input.
spokenForms.launch-from-input__s06-c1: Suppose the CPU input vector now contains nine values. Predict the element count, bytes per array and minimum number of four-thread blocks.
spokenForms.launch-from-input__s06-c2: Would changing only the block count provide larger GPU allocations or update the kernel argument? Pause and connect each setting to the data that supplies it.
spokenForms.launch-from-input__s07-c1: The vector supplies a count of nine. Nine times four gives thirty-six bytes for each array. Three blocks of four create twelve threads, with indices nine through eleven excluded.
spokenForms.launch-from-input__s07-c2: The program must provide the larger allocations, byte-counted copies and count argument too. Launch dimensions alone cannot update these separate responsibilities.
spokenForms.launch-from-input__s08-c1: The input array supplies the count. The operation determines the output shape. From those choices, the CPU program supplies storage, copies and launch arguments.
spokenForms.launch-from-input__s08-c2: Return to Chapter Three and trace its complete program. For later reductions or matrix operations, derive the required output size from that operation instead of assuming it always equals the input length.
spokenForms.layout__s01-c1: Chapter Five follows the selected values into storage. An element offset counts values from the start of that storage, beginning at zero.
spokenForms.layout__s01-c2: Our five by five F P thirty two tensor stores one row after another: row-major order. Each value uses four bytes. Large labels show values; small labels show element offsets.
spokenForms.layout__s02-c1: Selecting row zero makes a view into the original storage. Its five values occupy consecutive element offsets. Making this view copies no values.
spokenForms.layout__s02-c2: Stride is the distance, in elements, between successive selected values. Here stride one means four bytes. A byte offset measures distance in bytes from the storage's start.
spokenForms.layout__s03-c1: Column zero uses offsets zero, five, ten, fifteen and twenty. The next selected value is five element positions away, so this view has stride five.
spokenForms.layout__s03-c2: Five F P thirty two elements span twenty bytes, so its byte stride is twenty. The highlighted values stay in the original storage; selecting the column has not moved them together.
spokenForms.layout__s04-c1: Choose column one instead. Its first selected value begins one element into the same storage. The starting offset changes, but the stride remains five.
spokenForms.layout__s04-c2: Changing the column index still gives a view. To put the selected values next to one another, we need a different layout in separate storage.
spokenForms.layout__s05-c1: Calling contiguous on this column creates a packed copy: a new buffer with the same selected values in consecutive positions. The original storage is unchanged.
spokenForms.layout__s05-c2: The copy has stride one and new element offsets zero through four. Five four-byte values mean twenty bytes of values copied; copying also reads and writes memory.
spokenForms.layout__s06-c1: A row already has consecutive values. In row one, they begin at offset five and have stride one. Calling contiguous can return this row without copying.
spokenForms.layout__s06-c2: Contiguous describes the order of the values. A contiguous view can share another tensor's storage and start at a non-zero offset; it need not own a separate buffer.
spokenForms.layout__s07-c1: Now take column three and make a packed copy. Predict the new copy's element offsets and stride. Do its offsets keep the original column's starting position?
spokenForms.layout__s07-c2: How many bytes of values are copied, and does the original tensor change? Use the four-byte value size, then pause and explain before checking.
spokenForms.layout__s08-c1: The new buffer starts at its own offset zero. Its five element offsets are zero through four, with stride one. Twenty bytes of values are copied.
spokenForms.layout__s08-c2: The original tensor, selected values and multiplication results are unchanged. Return to Chapter Five and compare a view with a packed copy, separating layout, copy cost and measured performance.
spokenForms.matmul__s01-c1: Matrix multiplication combines inputs with weights in a neural network. Start with the four by four matrices from Chapter Ten.
spokenForms.matmul__s01-c2: One output combines a row from matrix [A](/ˈeɪ/) with a column from matrix B. The K index selects the matching pair of inputs.
spokenForms.matmul__s01-c3: This is our teaching algorithm. PyTorch selects its own implementation for the matrix operation.
spokenForms.matmul__s02-c1: For row zero and column zero, multiply each matching pair, then add the four products. The output is one point zero.
spokenForms.matmul__s02-c2: Our first algorithm gives each output its own thread. Each thread loads both inputs for every product.
spokenForms.matmul__s02-c3: Neighbouring outputs need some of the same inputs. Could a block load those inputs once and share them?
spokenForms.matmul__s03-c1: A tile is a small rectangular part of a matrix. Choose a two by two output tile, with one output per thread in our block.
spokenForms.matmul__s03-c2: Load both input tiles into shared memory: four values from matrix [A](/ˈeɪ/), and four from matrix B. These cover K positions zero and one.
spokenForms.matmul__s03-c3: This group of K positions is one phase. The four threads use the input tiles to build four partial sums.
spokenForms.matmul__s04-c1: Follow the highlighted value from matrix [A](/ˈeɪ/): minus two, at row zero and K zero.
spokenForms.matmul__s04-c2: It combines with two different values from matrix B, contributing to output columns zero and one in the same row.
spokenForms.matmul__s04-c3: The block keeps the input in shared memory so both threads can use it. Our count includes both products, even when one is zero.
spokenForms.matmul__s05-c1: Now follow minus one from matrix B, at K zero and column zero.
spokenForms.matmul__s05-c2: It combines with different values from matrix [A](/ˈeɪ/), contributing to output rows zero and one in the same column.
spokenForms.matmul__s05-c3: Each loaded value serves two outputs in this phase. The two input tiles contain eight values; separate output threads would load sixteen inputs for those same products.
spokenForms.matmul__s06-c1: We have included only the first two K positions. Each thread retains its own partial output sum while the block moves to the next phase.
spokenForms.matmul__s06-c2: The shared input tiles can be replaced only after every thread using them has finished. A real shared-memory implementation needs ordering between these uses and writes.
spokenForms.matmul__s06-c3: The new input tiles must also be ready before threads read them, applying the barrier reasoning from Chapter Nine.
spokenForms.matmul__s07-c1: The next input tiles cover K positions two and three. Their products are added to the existing partial sums.
spokenForms.matmul__s07-c2: For output row zero, column zero, the first phase contributed two. The second contributes minus one, leaving one point zero.
spokenForms.matmul__s07-c3: All four K positions are now included. This output tile matches the separate-output algorithm. The remaining output tiles follow the same pattern.

spokenForms.pattern-investigation__s01-c1: The final investigation combines the patterns around one output contract. Preparing grouped inputs also needs the token identities and their required order.

The opening PyTorch program requests stable sorting indices and gathers identities with them. PyTorch chooses its implementation. spokenForms.pattern-investigation__s02-c1: A histogram supplies the completed category counts. An exclusive scan of those counts gives each category's starting output position, called its bin start. The regions are disjoint: each bin reserves exactly its count of output positions.
spokenForms.pattern-investigation__s02-c2: The bin starts in the picture come from counts of earlier categories. They locate category regions, but not individual tokens inside them. Complete these counts and starts before dependent placement begins. The output has room for all eight identities; this model has no dropping or expert capacity limit.
spokenForms.pattern-investigation__s03-c1: Within-category rank counts earlier input tokens with the same category. Token five belongs to the first category and has two earlier peers. Its completed bin start plus its rank gives the highlighted output slot. The partial output shows only placements inspected so far.

spokenForms.pattern-investigation__s06-c1: All tokens now share one region. Their ranks count earlier tokens, so stable placement keeps the original identities in order. spokenForms.pipelines__s01-c1: The opening program processes two independent chunks in PyTorch. Each stream queues its copy before computation. Both streams finish before CPU results are collected. Keeping storage alive is necessary, but does not prove overlap. This opening program does not reuse an input slot.
spokenForms.pipelines__s01-c2: Double buffering uses two reusable slots. The browser adds abstract equal chunks, each with its own copy and computation. A ready event marks copy completion. A consumed event follows the actual consumer kernel. Later copies must wait for consumption before putting new inputs into that slot.
spokenForms.pipelines__s02-c1: This is a synthetic schedule, not GPU time. Copies take two arbitrary units; computation takes three. Each engine handles one operation at a time. Bar numbers identify chunks. The slot lanes show when each buffer is held, from copy start through consumer completion.
spokenForms.pipelines__s02-c2: In serial mode, each copy waits for the preceding computation as well as its engine and slot. Four chunks finish in twenty units. The time axis is shared with the next picture. Changing chunk count adds equal chunks; it does not repartition the opening program's eight values.
spokenForms.pipelines__s03-c1: Allow different engines to overlap, keeping every input and duration unchanged. Copying the next chunk can overlap computation on an earlier chunk. Operations on the same engine remain separate, and each computation still follows its own copy.
spokenForms.pipelines__s03-c2: Chunk two reuses the first slot. Its previous consumer still owns the buffer after the copy engine becomes free. That consumer releases the slot at five, which sets the next copy's start. The complete overlapping schedule takes fourteen synthetic units. The diagram shows dependencies, not a measured GPU speedup.
spokenForms.pipelines__s04-c1: Follow the highlighted chunk from ready to consumed. Its copy finishes before the compute queue becomes free. Ready therefore supplies the input, but does not let computation start early. Consumed follows the end of the actual computation, and only then permits reuse of that slot.
spokenForms.pipelines__s04-c2: A stream waiting for an event orders future queued work without making the CPU wait. Queuing a kernel is not its completion. Place the consumed marker after the real consumer launch in that stream. Keep pinned host inputs alive and unchanged until their transfers finish; a Python reference alone does not order overlapping writes.
spokenForms.pipelines__s05-c1: Keep four equal chunks, two reusable slots and computation duration three. Change only the copy duration to four synthetic units. Predict the completion total and which engine now sets the steady pace.
spokenForms.pipelines__s05-c2: For chunk two, compare the copy engine's availability with slot zero's release by chunk zero. Which constraint now delays the copy? Apply both handoffs and explain your reasoning before the comparison.
spokenForms.pipelines__s06-c1: The longer copies make the copy engine set the steady pace. For the highlighted chunk, the previous consumer releases its slot before that engine becomes free. Copying must still wait for the engine. The completed schedule takes nineteen synthetic units, with every computation following its own ready input.
spokenForms.pipelines__s06-c2: These totals belong to the declared model. Real overlap depends on hardware, pinned storage, stream dependencies and workload size. First compare outputs with a serial reference. Define the timed scope, warm up, measure completed work and inspect a profiler trace. spokenForms.progress__s01-c1: Chapter Eighteen asks whether a dependency can actually finish. A consumer needs its producer's result, and that producer must have an opportunity to run. Same-stream ordering handles the opening PyTorch example; the diagrams study separate coordination problems.
spokenForms.progress__s01-c2: Dining philosophers illustrates exclusive resource ownership. A, B and C each need the two numbered forks shown. Only one philosopher owns a fork at a time. Our ordered policy takes the lower number first, then the higher. Each philosopher eats once and releases both.
spokenForms.progress__s02-c1: Inspect the chosen execution. Each unfinished philosopher gets one opportunity per round. [A](/ˈeɪ/) holds fork zero and needs fork one. B owns forks one and two. C needs fork zero. The arrows point from a requester to the current owner of the fork it needs.
spokenForms.progress__s02-c2: B can eat at its next opportunity, release both forks and finish. [A](/ˈeɪ/) can then obtain its second fork; C finishes later. A common resource order prevents a circular resource wait. This finite example does not prove fairness or freedom from starvation in every scheduler.
spokenForms.progress__s03-c1: Deadlock means unfinished activities cannot progress because each needs another blocked activity to satisfy its wait. Change only the acquisition policy: each philosopher takes its own numbered fork first, and keeps it while waiting for the second.
spokenForms.progress__s03-c2: [A](/ˈeɪ/) now waits for B, B waits for C, and C waits for [A](/ˈeɪ/). Nobody holds both forks, so nobody can eat and release one. Another round of waiting changes no ownership. These are chosen ownership transitions, not a prediction of CPU or GPU scheduling.
spokenForms.progress__s04-c1: A block barrier is a different agreement. In this block of four threads, no thread exits early. All must reach the matching barrier before continuing. The valid diagram shows four arrivals and permission for the block to continue.
spokenForms.progress__s04-c2: In the diagnostic, threads two and three skip the call but continue elsewhere. Their missing arrivals violate the participation rule. Report invalid participation, not a numeric result or a guaranteed hardware hang. Resource ordering cannot repair a non-uniform barrier call.
spokenForms.progress__s05-c1: Consider two ordinary blocks and room for only one resident block in this illustration. Block [A](/ˈeɪ/) occupies that capacity while repeatedly checking a flag. Block B has not started, and only B can set the flag.
spokenForms.progress__s05-c2: Suppose all resource acquisitions follow a common order. Has that solved the progress dependency? Explain which block must run and which capacity it needs. Would a block barrier let the other block start? Pause before comparing your reasoning.
spokenForms.progress__s06-c1: Resource order does not make the unscheduled producer run. [A](/ˈeɪ/) is waiting for B while occupying the only slot B needs. Ordinary blocks have no general simultaneous-residency guarantee, and a block barrier cannot synchronise different blocks.
spokenForms.progress__s06-c2: Queue producer and consumer kernels in the same [CUDA](/ˈkuːdə/) stream, or express an appropriate dependency between streams. The consumer uses results after producer completion; queuing the launches does not make the CPU wait. Other documented collectives have their own launch requirements. Return to the chapter to distinguish resource cycles, missing barrier arrivals and scheduling dependencies. These diagrams measure no GPU time.

spokenForms.putting-it-together__s02-c2: Every choice produces the same complete output matrix in this model. These are explicit algorithm loads with cache reuse excluded; they are not measured physical memory traffic.
spokenForms.putting-it-together__s03-c1: With the chapter’s synthetic resource budgets, tile width two uses thirty-two shared-memory bytes and two hundred and fifty-six registers per block. Four blocks fit those budgets.

spokenForms.putting-it-together__s04-c2: Either tile can be a hypothesis worth investigating. Neither a lower load count nor a higher block capacity proves which implementation is faster on a physical GPU.
spokenForms.putting-it-together__s05-c1: Now use eight-by-eight inputs with tile width two and the same resource budgets. Predict input loads, output stores and resident-block capacity.
spokenForms.putting-it-together__s05-c2: Does doubling the matrix dimension double every count? Separate complete-operation counts from resources needed by one block before comparing the answer.
spokenForms.putting-it-together__s06-c1: This eight-by-eight case loads five hundred and twelve input values and stores sixty-four outputs. Four blocks still fit the stated teaching budgets.
spokenForms.putting-it-together__s06-c2: At fixed tile width, input loads grow with the cube of the matrix dimension, while output stores grow with its square. The resources used by one block do not change here.
spokenForms.putting-it-together__s07-c1: To compare real implementations, first check both outputs against a suitable reference. Keep inputs and number format comparable, and change one proposed optimisation at a time.
spokenForms.putting-it-together__s07-c2: Define whether timing includes allocation and transfers. Warm up, wait for the GPU work in the chosen interval, repeat measurements, and inspect actual operations with a profiler.

spokenForms.reading__s01-c1: Chapter Four keeps the floating-point values on the GPU and arranges them in a five by five tensor. Row and column numbers start at zero.
spokenForms.reading__s01-c2: The first coordinate selects a row; the second selects a column. These logical coordinates identify inputs. PyTorch chooses execution details for the [CUDA](/ˈkuːdə/) operation.
spokenForms.reading__s02-c1: Read x, zero, colon. Row zero is fixed, while the colon includes all columns. Trace the five highlighted inputs from left to right.
spokenForms.reading__s02-c2: Selecting the row chooses the inputs. Multiplying each selected value by two is a separate calculation, which we will inspect next.
spokenForms.reading__s03-c1: Each output is twice its selected input. The source coordinates beside the values show where every input came from in the original tensor.
spokenForms.reading__s03-c2: This multiplication creates a new result tensor. It leaves the original x unchanged. Selecting a row and calculating its outputs are different parts of the expression.
spokenForms.reading__s04-c1: Now read x, colon, zero. The column is fixed, while the colon includes all rows. We take one input from each row.
spokenForms.reading__s04-c2: The first row and first column share their first value, but the other inputs differ. Both selections still contain five values.
spokenForms.reading__s05-c1: Multiply each column input by two. Each result uses one highlighted input; we are not adding the five values into a single total.
spokenForms.reading__s05-c2: This is elementwise multiplication: apply the operation separately to each selected value. Changing from a row to a column changes the inputs, while the multiplier stays fixed.
spokenForms.reading__s06-c1: With index one, a row selection chooses the second row. A column selection chooses the second column. Compare their five inputs in the diagram.

spokenForms.reading__s07-c2: Trace the five input cells, then predict their five outputs. Does index three mean the fourth row or the fourth column here? Pause and explain.
spokenForms.reading__s08-c1: Index three fixes the fourth column because counting starts at zero. The colon includes every row. The diagram follows those five inputs into their doubled results.
spokenForms.reading__s08-c2: The original tensor is unchanged. Return to Chapter Four, change only a row or column index, and explain the selected inputs before pressing Run.
spokenForms.reduction__s01-c1: A sum combines values handled by different threads. Follow the four inputs from Chapter Nine: one, two, three and four.
spokenForms.reduction__s01-c2: There are four threads in one block. A block is a group whose threads can cooperate. Each thread has one input.
spokenForms.reduction__s01-c3: This is our teaching algorithm for the sum, not a trace of the implementation PyTorch selects.
spokenForms.reduction__s02-c1: Each thread starts with its own input. To exchange values, the block uses shared memory: storage its threads can read and write.
spokenForms.reduction__s02-c2: Each four-byte storage position is a word. Thread zero writes its input, one point zero, into shared word zero.
spokenForms.reduction__s02-c3: The other words are still unwritten in this snapshot. The thread numbers and word indices start at zero.
spokenForms.reduction__s03-c1: Now inspect the state after all four input writes. Shared words zero through three hold one, two, three and four.
spokenForms.reduction__s03-c2: We display those writes in an inspection order. A real program cannot rely on threads reaching their instructions in this order.
spokenForms.reduction__s03-c3: Before a thread reads its partner's value, the program must establish that the write comes first.
spokenForms.reduction__s04-c1: A block barrier provides that ordering. All four threads must reach it before any continues beyond it.
spokenForms.reduction__s04-c2: The barrier also orders shared-memory accesses. Preceding writes become visible to the block's threads after the barrier.
spokenForms.reduction__s04-c3: This does not wait for other blocks. It orders cooperation within this block, including the writes needed by our first additions.
spokenForms.reduction__s05-c1: For four inputs, the first partner distance is two. Thread zero adds shared word two to its own word: one plus three makes four.
spokenForms.reduction__s05-c2: Thread one adds shared word three: two plus four makes six.
spokenForms.reduction__s05-c3: The partial sums are written into words zero and one. Their input-index labels show that the two pairs have no input in common.
spokenForms.reduction__s06-c1: The next addition needs the new partial sum from thread one. We therefore need another block barrier after the partial-sum writes.
spokenForms.reduction__s06-c2: Threads two and three perform no addition in this stage. They still reach the barrier with the other threads.
spokenForms.reduction__s06-c3: The barrier belongs after the conditional addition, where every thread can reach it. It must not be restricted to just the adding threads.
spokenForms.reduction__s07-c1: The partner distance is now one. Thread zero combines four and six, producing ten in shared word zero.
spokenForms.reduction__s07-c2: Follow the input-index labels: the final sum contains indices zero, two, one and three, each exactly once.
spokenForms.reduction__s07-c3: The arrows express dependencies between values. They do not show GPU clock cycles or promise that the drawn operations execute simultaneously.
spokenForms.reduction__s08-c1: Now remove the synchronisation. In this diagnostic, thread zero writes its own input, then reads shared word two before thread two writes there.
spokenForms.reduction__s08-c2: The partner word is unwritten. There is no valid partial sum to display.
spokenForms.reduction__s08-c3: This is one possible interleaving exposing a data race: conflicting accesses without the required ordering, including a write. We assign no numeric result to the racy program.
spokenForms.reduction__s09-c1: Thread two eventually writes three point zero. That does not repair the read that already happened.
spokenForms.reduction__s09-c2: Putting a barrier only after the early read cannot fix it either. The input writes must be ordered before partner reads, and partial-sum writes before the next stage's reads.
spokenForms.reduction__s09-c3: Even a plausible answer from another execution would not establish that the program is safe.
spokenForms.reduction__s10-c1: Try a new case with eight inputs and eight threads in one block. The first partner distance is four, so only threads zero through three add.
spokenForms.reduction__s10-c2: How many threads must reach the block barrier after those additions?
spokenForms.reduction__s10-c3: Which thread supplies the value that thread one reads first? Pause here and explain your answers.
spokenForms.reduction__s11-c1: All eight threads must reach the block barrier. That includes the four threads that did no addition.
spokenForms.reduction__s11-c2: Thread one first reads shared word five. Thread five's input write must precede that read; the initial barrier establishes the ordering.
spokenForms.reduction__s11-c3: Return to Chapter Nine. Set the input count to eight and inspect the tree. Follow the writes, barriers and partner distances. Explain each read using the write that supplies its value.
spokenForms.requests__s01-c1: Chapter Six connects tensor layout to memory requests. In this teaching example, five threads each read one F P thirty two input for the same multiplication.
spokenForms.requests__s01-c2: A warp has thirty-two thread positions, called lanes. Only lanes zero through four read here. The other twenty-seven positions make no read; this is a chosen mapping, not a captured PyTorch launch.
spokenForms.requests__s02-c1: A sector is an aligned thirty-two-byte region used to group the input reads. Aligned boundaries occur at byte offsets zero, thirty-two, sixty-four, and so on.
spokenForms.requests__s02-c2: Each F P thirty two value uses four bytes, so eight consecutive values fit inside one sector. Both the original tensor and any packed allocation start on a sector boundary in this example.
spokenForms.requests__s03-c1: Row zero occupies element offsets zero through four. Its five reads begin at byte offsets zero, four, eight, twelve and sixteen. All belong to sector zero.
spokenForms.requests__s03-c2: The threads request twenty useful bytes. One touched sector covers thirty-two bytes. Covered bytes describe the regions containing these reads; they are not additional tensor data.
spokenForms.requests__s04-c1: Column zero selects element offsets zero, five, ten, fifteen and twenty. Multiply each offset by four to find its byte position, then group by sector.
spokenForms.requests__s04-c2: Threads zero and one share sector zero. Threads two and three share sector one. Thread four reaches sector two. There are still twenty useful bytes, but the three sectors cover ninety-six bytes.
spokenForms.requests__s05-c1: The packed copy contains the same five column values in a new allocation. Its reads begin at byte offsets zero through sixteen, stepping by four, so they share one sector.
spokenForms.requests__s05-c2: This comparison counts one input read. It excludes the reads and writes that make the packed copy, and excludes output stores. Fewer touched sectors alone do not establish that packing is faster overall.
spokenForms.requests__s06-c1: Now choose row one. Its five values are neighbours, but they occupy element offsets five through nine, or byte positions twenty through thirty-nine.
spokenForms.requests__s06-c2: The first three reads belong to sector zero; the last two belong to sector one. Twenty useful bytes now touch two sectors. Consecutive values do not guarantee a single sector: the starting position matters.
spokenForms.requests__s07-c1: Apply the same rule to row three. The original storage is still sector aligned, and each value still occupies four bytes. Predict which sectors contain its five reads.
spokenForms.requests__s07-c2: How many useful bytes and covered bytes should the model report? Pause and group the byte positions before checking the answer.
spokenForms.requests__s08-c1: Row three starts at byte sixty. Its first read belongs to sector one; the remaining four belong to sector two. That is twenty useful bytes and sixty-four covered bytes.
spokenForms.requests__s08-c2: Return to Chapter Six and explain why alignment changes the count. These are addressed sectors for one modelled input read, not physical DRAM transactions, cache misses or elapsed GPU time.
spokenForms.scan__s01-c1: Chapter Sixteen starts with the same token categories. A flag is one when its token is selected and zero otherwise. A histogram gives a total, but placement also needs the number of selected tokens before each input.
spokenForms.scan__s01-c2: A prefix sum, or scan, keeps a total for every position. Inclusive prefixes include the current flag. Exclusive prefixes count only earlier flags, so a selected token can use its exclusive prefix as an output destination.
spokenForms.scan__s02-c1: Our teaching algorithm uses one block and a separate old and new shared array. At partner distance one, a thread reads its own old value and its preceding neighbour's old value, when that neighbour exists.
spokenForms.scan__s02-c2: Position three adds the flags at positions three and two. It writes one into the new snapshot. All threads finish the stage and reach a barrier before the next stage reads that snapshot. No thread reads a neighbour's new write within the same stage.
spokenForms.scan__s03-c1: The next stage reads only the completed previous snapshot. Position three combines two partial counts from positions three and one. Each partial contains a single selected flag, so their combined total is two and covers the first four input flags.
spokenForms.scan__s03-c2: For eight inputs a later distance-four stage combines larger groups. Positions without a partner keep their value but still participate in the barrier. Distances describe dependencies, not GPU clock cycles. PyTorch may choose a different scan algorithm.
spokenForms.scan__s04-c1: The inclusive result includes each position's own flag. At position five, that includes the selected token itself. Its exclusive offset instead counts only earlier selected tokens, giving that token its destination in a packed output.
spokenForms.scan__s04-c2: Shifting the completed inclusive array right and inserting zero constructs these exclusive offsets. Production code need not use a separate shift. The output length is the last exclusive offset plus the last flag, so a final selected token is not lost.
spokenForms.scan__s05-c1: Now keep only the first four input flags, with the same rules for one block. Predict which partner distances are needed. Which distance was required for eight flags but is unnecessary for four?
spokenForms.scan__s05-c2: Derive the exclusive offsets. Then use the last offset and last flag to determine the output length. Name which input positions would write. Pause before revealing the comparison.
spokenForms.scan__s06-c1: Four inputs need partner distances one and two. Distance four is unnecessary. The exclusive offsets are zero, one, one and two. Positions zero and two are selected, so they write destinations zero and one.
spokenForms.scan__s06-c2: The last offset is two and the last flag is zero, giving output length two. Return to the chapter to inspect snapshot dependencies and explain why a skipped token may share an offset without performing a write. Multiple blocks need an additional ordered combination of block totals.
spokenForms.scheduling__s01-c1: Chapter Seven asks what can run while a warp waits for data. A load brings an input into a thread's registers. The multiply uses that working value, and a store writes the result to memory.
spokenForms.scheduling__s01-c2: Our teaching scheduler gives each resident warp two repetitions of load, multiply, store. Resident means already assigned resources on one streaming multiprocessor, or S M. This chosen instruction stream does not trace PyTorch's implementation or compute its tensor values.
spokenForms.scheduling__s02-c1: A model cycle is one discrete step. Our machine can start at most one instruction per cycle. Load latency six means the dependent multiply cannot start until six cycles after its load.
spokenForms.scheduling__s02-c2: Warp zero starts its load at cycle zero. At cycles one through five it is waiting, so the issue slots are idle. The multiply starts at cycle six. These cycles are teaching assumptions, not measured GPU time.
spokenForms.scheduling__s03-c1: Now begin with two resident warps, both ready at cycle zero. The scheduler selects warp zero first, then searches from the following warp for the next ready instruction.
spokenForms.scheduling__s03-c2: At cycle one, warp zero is waiting but warp one is ready. Warp one starts its load. The S M can issue useful work while another warp waits; it does not need a separate arithmetic unit for each warp.
spokenForms.scheduling__s04-c1: At cycle two, both warps are waiting for their loaded inputs. Neither can start its multiply, so this issue slot is idle. Cycles three through five are idle too.
spokenForms.scheduling__s04-c2: Another resident warp helps only when it has an instruction ready to start. This scheduler skips waiting and completed warps. It never leaves a slot idle when an unfinished warp is ready.
spokenForms.scheduling__s05-c1: At cycle six, warp zero's first load is usable. Warp one's load started a cycle later, so it is still waiting. The scheduler starts warp zero's multiply.
spokenForms.scheduling__s05-c2: At cycle seven, warp one becomes ready and starts its multiply. The cards show state before the selected instruction starts. Registers belong to threads; the execution hardware is shared by resident warps.
spokenForms.scheduling__s06-c1: Keep load latency at six and compare one, two and four resident warps. Idle slots fall from ten to eight to four. Four warps still do not fill every wait in this example.
spokenForms.scheduling__s06-c2: Each warp adds six instructions, so issued work rises from six to twelve to twenty-four. These different workloads do not establish a speedup. The model ends when the final store starts, without a later store-completion wait.
spokenForms.scheduling__s07-c1: Apply the readiness rule to a new case: two resident warps, with load latency three instead of six. Warp zero loads at cycle zero and warp one loads at cycle one.
spokenForms.scheduling__s07-c2: Predict whether cycle two is idle. Then choose which warp can start its multiply at cycle three. Pause and explain using the load start times, before checking the answer.
spokenForms.scheduling__s08-c1: At cycle two, neither load is ready, so the slot is idle. At cycle three, warp zero's input is usable, while warp one must wait until cycle four. Warp zero starts its multiply.
spokenForms.scheduling__s08-c2: Return to Chapter Seven and distinguish a waiting warp from an idle issue slot. This single-issue, round-robin machine omits resource-limited residency, bandwidth competition and real instruction latencies. More resident warps alone do not prove higher GPU performance.
spokenForms.tensor-cores__s01-c1: Chapter Eleven separates input representation from accumulation. Our matrix [A](/ˈeɪ/) repeats one row sixteen times; matrix B contains only ones, so every output uses the same row sum.
spokenForms.tensor-cores__s01-c2: The row begins with eight values written as one point zero zero zero three, followed by eight negative ones. They enter F P thirty two storage first, then convert to F P sixteen or B F sixteen. Each smaller format uses two bytes per input instead of four.
